messages.content: I am looking into issue #1421 regarding the deprecation of request.json in Flask. The community seems split on whether to keep it or force users toward request.get_json(). I am currently reviewing the implementation in flask/wrappers.py. What is your take on the current API surface for JSON handling?

The challenge with request.json is that it conflates a property access with a method call that might fail. In flask/wrappers.py, the current implementation masks parsing errors by returning None, which is problematic for strict API implementations. If we shift to requiring request.get_json(), we gain the ability to pass silent=False or force=True, providing much better feedback to the developer when a payload is malformed.

That makes sense. If I modify Request.json in flask/wrappers.py to issue a stacklevel-aware DeprecationWarning, how should I handle the performance impact of checking this on every request? I am worried about the overhead if this is called in a high-traffic environment.

You are right to be concerned about the overhead in flask/wrappers.py. A direct warning inside the property getter will fire on every access. I suggest we wrap the warning in a context that checks if the request is already processed, or perhaps leverage the warnings module filters to suppress it in production settings. Alternatively, we could perform the warning only if a specific debug flag is set.

Let's try a conditional check in flask/wrappers.py. I'll implement a hidden attribute _warned_json_access to ensure we only warn once per request object lifecycle. I suspect this will keep the runtime cost negligible while still alerting developers to the pending removal of the API.

That approach sounds efficient. When modifying flask/wrappers.py, ensure you are using warnings.warn with stacklevel=2 so the trace points to the user's code, not the framework internals. Did you consider how this impacts testing? I anticipate tests in tests/test_helpers.py might start failing due to unhandled warnings.

Good catch. I ran the test suite and tests/test_helpers.py is indeed triggering errors with warnings.simplefilter('error'). I will need to update the test suite to either catch these specific warnings or explicitly use request.get_json() in the tests to future-proof the codebase.

Updating tests/test_helpers.py to use request.get_json() is the correct path forward for a clean refactor. It serves as documentation for users as well. Once those are updated, check if any internal extensions rely on request.json. If they do, those must be patched simultaneously to avoid breaking existing downstream users.

I checked flask/ext/ (legacy extensions) and identified a few references. I will submit a PR that cleans these up alongside the core change in flask/wrappers.py. I am also thinking about adding a documentation note in docs/api.rst to make the migration path clear for users of the stable branch.

That comprehensive approach will be well-received by the maintainers. Updating docs/api.rst is crucial for the 1.x to 2.0 transition. Before you push, verify the behavior in flask/wrappers.py when the content-type is missing. We should ensure that calling request.get_json() doesn't raise unnecessary errors if the intent was just to inspect the payload.

I have verified the behavior in flask/wrappers.py. Calling request.get_json(silent=True) handles missing content-types gracefully by returning None. My new implementation will respect the silent parameter correctly. I will now run the integration tests in tests/test_reqctx.py to ensure the request context is properly maintained during the transition.

Excellent. Keep an eye on the RequestContext lifecycle. If request.json was used in a context-local way, moving to a method call should not affect the storage. Ensure that the proxy object in flask/globals.py continues to point to the correct instance even if the user switches to the method approach.

I've confirmed the proxy in flask/globals.py remains stable. The transition seems safe. I've finished the changes in flask/wrappers.py and verified that running the tests with --warn-all shows the DeprecationWarning exactly where expected. The fix seems robust.

Great progress. How did you handle the DeprecationWarning suppression in your test environment? Did you use the pytest.warns context manager in tests/test_reqctx.py, or did you create a custom marker for the legacy tests?

I used pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning) in tests/test_reqctx.py. It felt cleaner than a global filter. This way, I can isolate the specific areas where we are still testing legacy behavior without silencing warnings for new features. I'm happy with this coverage.

That is a clean solution. One final check: does the documentation in docs/api.rst clarify the 'force' parameter? Many users incorrectly assume request.get_json() needs the content-type header, but 'force=True' overrides that. Make sure the deprecation note emphasizes that power.

Yes, I added a paragraph in docs/api.rst explaining the 'force' and 'silent' parameters. It should significantly reduce confusion for users migrating from the older property-based syntax. I'm ready to open the PR for the core changes.

Everything looks solid. Before submitting, do a quick grep for 'request.json' across the entire repository one last time to ensure no hidden usages in examples or snippets in the docs folder that I might have missed. If that comes up clean, you are good to go.

Ran a full-text search. Everything looks clear. I found one snippet in examples/tutorial/ but that has been patched. The project structure seems clean for this deprecation. Thank you for the guidance on the implementation details and the test suite integration.

You are very welcome. This is a significant improvement for the Flask API. By handling the deprecation cycle with warnings and proper documentation updates, you have ensured a much smoother transition for the user base. Good luck with the pull request review!

Wait, I just triggered a secondary issue while running the full test suite. It looks like the Werkzeug integration in flask/wrappers.py might be failing when I pass the force=True parameter in environments with strict type checking. Is it possible that the underlying Request class is not propagating the boolean correctly through the middleware?

That is a suspicious finding. Check the Request class inheritance in flask/wrappers.py. If we are wrapping a Werkzeug Request, ensure the 'get_json' method is correctly delegated. It is possible that the 'force' flag is being swallowed by a superclass call that does not expect that signature.

You are right. I looked at the call stack, and it seems that the base Werkzeug class is calling 'on_json_loading_failed'. I am getting a 'TypeError: unexpected keyword argument' during the execution of my new tests in tests/test_reqctx.py. I suspect the version of Werkzeug in my dev environment might have a different method signature than I anticipated.

Ah, check the requirements.txt file. We are currently targeting a specific version of Werkzeug. If your local install updated, it might have introduced breaking changes. Try pinning the version explicitly and see if the signature mismatch in flask/wrappers.py persists.

Good catch. My local environment drifted to a newer Werkzeug master build. After pinning back to the project version, the 'TypeError' in flask/wrappers.py disappeared. However, I am now seeing a regression in how 'request.json' caches its result. It seems like multiple calls are triggering redundant parsing.

That points to the state management inside the Request object. Look at how we memoize the JSON result in flask/wrappers.py. Are we using a private attribute like '_cached_json'? If the property access is deprecated, we need to ensure the new 'get_json' call properly populates that cache.

I see it now. In flask/wrappers.py, the 'get_json' function was resetting '_cached_json' every time 'cache=True' was passed, even if it was already set. I am refactoring that logic to check for the cache before parsing the request data stream. This should solve the redundant parsing issue.

Smart move. Make sure that your check handles the case where the cache might be set to 'None' intentionally (e.g., if parsing failed earlier). Add a test case in tests/test_reqctx.py specifically for repeated calls to 'request.get_json()' to verify the cache behavior is now idempotent.

Added the test case and it passed. I verified the caching mechanism by adding a print statement inside the parser function. Now it only prints once per request. The performance overhead is eliminated. I am feeling much more confident about this implementation now.

That is excellent. A performance regression here would have been a dealbreaker for high-traffic Flask apps. Have you verified that this doesn't conflict with any custom 'JSONDecoder' classes that users might register via 'app.json_decoder'?

I checked 'flask/app.py'. My implementation of 'get_json' respects the current app instance's decoder. I am pulling the decoder from the current context, which is the standard way to handle custom serialization in Flask. It looks safe for users who have customized their serialization logic.

Great, that maintains backward compatibility with user-defined configuration. Are you running these tests against multiple Python versions? I remember 'flask' having some nuances with how 'json.loads' behaves between 3.6 and 3.9.

I have run 'tox' to cover the 3.7 through 3.11 range. Everything passed except for a minor warning in the older versions regarding bytes vs strings, but the 'get_json' output remains consistent. I am satisfied that the core logic is cross-version compatible.

Excellent work. Since 'tox' passed and the logic is verified across versions, you've definitely ironed out the wrinkles. Is there any remaining documentation cleanup needed in 'docs/api.rst' regarding these version-specific nuances?

I updated 'docs/api.rst' to include a 'versionadded' note for the deprecation and a 'note' about the performance optimization. It is ready for the maintainers to review the documentation changes alongside the code PR.

This seems like a complete solution. You have addressed the initial deprecation, fixed a regression, optimized caching, and ensured cross-version stability. You're ready to commit. Are you planning to squash your commits?

Yes, I will squash the 'fix' and 'test' commits into a single coherent change. It makes the history in the 'flask' repository much cleaner. I will follow the existing commit message convention: 'Deprecate request.json in favor of request.get_json()'.

Perfect naming convention. It follows the standard established in the 'pallets' project. Don't forget to link the original GitHub issue #1421 in the PR body. Do you have any final questions before you push to your fork?

No, I'm ready. I have double-checked the 'CONTRIBUTING.rst' file to make sure I am following the project's style guide. I feel good about this. Pushing to my branch 'feature/request-json-deprecation' now.
Fantastic. The team will appreciate the rigour you've applied to this task. Good luck with the PR submission, and I look forward to seeing this merged into the codebase!

I just pushed the branch to origin. Wait, I am seeing a failure in the CI pipeline for 'test_json_mimetype' in 'tests/test_helpers.py'. It looks like 'request.get_json' is failing when the content type isn't explicitly set to 'application/json', even though the payload is valid.

That is unexpected. Check the 'flask/wrappers.py' file where the 'Request' class implements the 'json' property. It might be that the strict mimetype checking logic was accidentally tightened during your refactoring of the caching mechanism.

You are right. In 'flask/wrappers.py', I changed the default 'force' argument to 'False' inside the 'get_json' method to be more explicit. This broke compatibility for older test cases where the mimetype wasn't explicitly provided in the mock request headers.

Exactly. Flask has historically been lenient with content types for 'request.json'. You should revert that default parameter to 'None' or 'False' only if you ensure the existing legacy behavior is preserved. Let's look at the implementation of '_load_json' in the same file.

I see it. I will adjust the '_load_json' internal call to respect a 'silent' parameter. If I keep 'force' as 'False' by default, I should allow users to bypass the check if they use 'get_json(force=True)'. I'll update 'flask/wrappers.py' now.

Good plan. Make sure you also update the docstring in 'flask/wrappers.py' for 'get_json' so future users know exactly how 'force' interacts with the 'application/json' header. Does this change affect the caching logic we implemented?

The caching logic in 'flask/wrappers.py' should stay the same. I'm storing the parsed result in 'self._cached_json'. If 'force' is True, I will bypass the cache check entirely to ensure the user gets fresh data based on their specific request. That should be safer.
That sounds like a robust approach. Testing that specific edge case in 'tests/test_helpers.py' is crucial. Can you add a test case that specifically toggles 'force' and asserts the cache is bypassed?

I added 'test_get_json_force_bypass' to 'tests/test_helpers.py'. It sets a dummy value in the cache, then performs a forced load. I'm checking that the cache is overwritten or ignored correctly. Running 'pytest' now locally.
Excellent, covering that logic explicitly will prevent future regressions. Are the tests passing now for both standard and forced scenarios?
Yes, all tests in 'tests/test_helpers.py' passed! The previous failure in 'test_json_mimetype' is also resolved because I adjusted the default behavior to match what it was before my changes.

Excellent. It sounds like you have addressed the regression successfully. Have you verified the performance impact of this fix? We don't want the cache bypass to create a performance bottleneck for normal requests.

I ran a quick benchmark using 'pytest-benchmark'. The overhead for standard requests remains unchanged since I only add a conditional check for the 'force' argument. The performance impact is negligible.

That is reassuring. The Flask maintainers will be pleased that you prioritized both correctness and performance. Do you need to update any other files, perhaps 'CHANGES.rst' to document this specific fix?

Yes, I should add a brief mention of the 'force' parameter refinement in 'CHANGES.rst'. It's important to be transparent about how we handled the mimetype compatibility for users relying on the old 'request.json' behavior.
Agreed. 'CHANGES.rst' is the canonical source for upgrade information. Once that's added, are you going to squash these new commits into your branch?
Yes, I'll squash the 'fix regression' commit with the original one. I'll make sure the commit message remains clean and descriptive. Everything seems ready to go.
Sounds like you are in a great spot. Go ahead and force-push to your branch, then leave a comment on the PR indicating that the CI failure has been resolved.
Done. Pushing now. I also updated the PR body on GitHub to link to the updated documentation and the specific tests that handle the mimetype edge cases.

Perfect. You have navigated a tricky regression and emerged with a cleaner, better-tested implementation. Your contribution to 'pallets/flask' looks very professional. Good luck with the final review!

I noticed a new comment from one of the Flask maintainers on the PR. They are asking about potential side effects if someone is using a custom request subclass that overrides 'get_json' in 'flask/wrappers.py'. Should I check that?

That is a valid concern. If users are extending 'Request' class, your changes to 'get_json' logic might not propagate as expected. You should add a test case in 'tests/test_request_ctx.py' that mocks a custom request class to verify behavior.
Good point. I will create a dummy class 'CustomRequest' inheriting from 'Request' and override 'get_json'. I'll see if calling 'request.get_json()' on that instance triggers my new logic correctly.
Exactly. Ensure that your new 'force' keyword argument is passed correctly through the inheritance chain. If 'get_json' is overridden without calling 'super()', it might break.

I just ran the tests with the new 'CustomRequest' case. It seems that if the subclass ignores '**kwargs', the 'force' parameter gets dropped. I should update the documentation to warn users about this.
Updating the docs is a good call, but maybe you can also provide a small helper or a recommendation in the docstring of 'flask/wrappers.py' to ensure proper delegation.
I've added a note to the docstring of the 'Request' class. It now explicitly states that overriding 'get_json' should always handle 'kwargs' to maintain future compatibility with signature changes.
That should mitigate the risk for users. Did you run the full suite again after modifying the docstring, just to ensure no linting errors popped up?
Yes, 'flake8' passed without issues. The documentation build also looks clean. I am feeling much more confident about this patch now.
Great. The PR status is currently 'CI passed'. I would suggest pinging the maintainers again on the GitHub issue tracker to signal that the custom subclass compatibility has been addressed.
I've left a comment detailing the 'CustomRequest' verification and the docstring update. I'm hopeful that this is the final hurdle for the review process.
Excellent work. While we wait, is there any other part of the request lifecycle that this change might inadvertently affect, perhaps multipart form data processing?

I've reviewed 'flask/wrappers.py' and 'flask/globals.py'. The 'request.json' logic is isolated enough that it shouldn't interfere with standard 'request.form' or file uploads. Everything seems decoupled.
That consistency is one of the strengths of Flask's design. If the isolation is that clear, there is very little risk of breaking existing multipart parsing.
I just received a notification that the PR has been approved by the core team. They suggested minor style nits in the commit message format.
The commit message style is often the final step in these reviews. Just ensure you follow the 'pallets' project conventions regarding the prefixing of commit titles.
I've adjusted the commit title to 'Fix: Refactor request.json parsing and add force argument support'. That should align better with their standards.
That looks perfect. Squashing and amending that message will finalize your history. Are you planning to delete the feature branch after the merge?
Yes, I'll clean up the local and remote branches once the merge is finalized. It's been a long journey for such a small change, but it was a great learning experience.
It is exactly that kind of attention to detail that ensures high-quality open-source projects. You have contributed a solid fix to the community. Congratulations on your work!

Now that the PR is merged into the main branch, I am running the full test suite locally using 'tox' to ensure no regressions were introduced by the squash merge. I noticed some linting warnings in 'tests/test_helpers.py' that I had not seen before.

Running 'tox' is a smart move. Those linting warnings might be artifacts of the latest 'flake8' updates in the environment. Check if 'tests/test_helpers.py' has any undefined imports or whitespace issues that conflict with the 'pallets' coding standards.

You were right. It looks like an unused import in 'tests/test_helpers.py' slipped through during my last rebase. I'm removing the 'warnings' module import now. Should I open a small follow-up PR, or just leave it for a general maintenance patch?

Given the project's strict stance on clean code, a small, focused PR labeled as 'chore: cleanup' for that import is usually appreciated. It keeps the commit history cleaner than mixing fixes with maintenance.

Agreed. I will create a branch named 'fix/cleanup-imports' and submit that quickly. While I am at it, should I update the documentation in 'docs/api.rst' to reflect the behavior changes in 'request.json' more explicitly?

That would be a great addition. Adding a 'versionadded' or 'versionchanged' directive in 'docs/api.rst' specifically for the 'force' parameter in 'request.get_json()' helps users transitioning from the deprecated 'request.json' property.

I am working on the Sphinx directives in 'docs/api.rst' now. I noticed that the current documentation for 'flask.Request' does not explicitly warn users away from 'request.json'. I think I should add an '.. deprecated:: 0.12' block.
That is a perfect use of the deprecation directive. Make sure to reference the GitHub issue link in the documentation text so users can track the rationale behind the change if they have questions.

Good call. I have updated 'docs/api.rst' to include the link. Now I am running 'make html' in the 'docs/' directory to verify that the documentation builds correctly and the deprecation warning appears as expected.
Checking the build output is vital. Ensure there are no broken cross-references or missing links introduced by the new directive. A failed build usually logs errors in 'docs/_build/linkcheck.txt'.
The build finished successfully without warnings. I am now pushing the documentation changes as a separate commit to the 'fix/cleanup-imports' branch. Should I include the docs update in the same PR?
Yes, grouping the documentation update with the minor linting cleanup is acceptable in this context. It essentially completes the 'request.json' deprecation task thoroughly.
PR #1425 is up. It includes the import fix in 'tests/test_helpers.py' and the documentation update in 'docs/api.rst'. I feel much better having the deprecation notice documented properly.
Excellent. Documenting deprecations is a crucial part of the lifecycle. Once this is merged, the 'request.json' deprecation will be fully supported by clear guidance for users.

The CI passed on the new PR. I am waiting for a maintainer to glance at it. While I wait, I've been looking at 'flask/wrappers.py' again. Is it worth adding a runtime warning via the 'warnings' module to 'request.json' itself?
Adding a 'warnings.warn' call with 'DeprecationWarning' is standard practice. It ensures that developers see the warning in their development logs without breaking production builds immediately.
I've added the warning to the '@property' decorator of 'request.json' in 'flask/wrappers.py'. It seems to work locally when I run a test script. The warning triggers exactly once per request cycle.
That is the correct behavior. By using the 'stacklevel' argument in 'warnings.warn', you ensure the warning points to the user's code, not the internal implementation of Flask.

I used 'stacklevel=2' as suggested by the 'warnings' documentation. This has been a very rewarding process, from the initial discussion to the final deprecation implementation. I am ready to close this out.
You have done a fantastic job. You handled the logic, the testing, the documentation, and the final deprecation warnings. Your contributions have definitely made Flask a cleaner, more robust library.

I noticed in the latest CI logs for PR #1425 that there is a slight performance overhead introduced by the new 'warnings.warn' call in 'flask/wrappers.py'. Should I be worried about this impacting production request handlers?

The overhead of 'warnings.warn' is negligible in most Flask applications. However, to be safe, you can wrap the call in a conditional check that only executes if the filter settings are currently set to report 'DeprecationWarning', which keeps it lean.

That is a great idea. I will modify 'flask/wrappers.py' to use a 'warnings.filterwarnings' check. Wait, actually, that might be too complex for a simple deprecation. Maybe I should just leave it as is, given the stability of the 'warnings' module?

Stick to the simplest implementation. 'warnings.warn' is highly optimized in CPython. Don't overengineer it, as readability in 'flask/wrappers.py' is more important than micro-optimizing a deprecation notice.

Agreed. I will keep the original implementation. I have verified that 'tests/test_wrappers.py' covers the warning correctly using 'pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning)'. The coverage report is still holding steady at 98 percent.
That level of test coverage is impressive. Having 'pytest.warns' confirm the deprecation behavior ensures that future changes to 'request.json' won't accidentally silence the warning.

I just received a ping from a maintainer on GitHub. They asked if the 'request.json' deprecation should be scoped to a specific version, like Flask 2.0. Should I update the 'docs/api.rst' file to reflect a version constraint?
Yes, you should explicitly mention the target version. Update the docstrings in 'flask/wrappers.py' and the 'docs/api.rst' file to specify that this will be removed in the next major release.
Done. I have updated the docstrings to reference 'Flask 2.0'. It feels much more professional to have that clear path forward. I'm pushing these changes to the 'fix/cleanup-imports' branch now.
The PR looks perfect now. The combination of code, tests, and clear documentation makes this a model contribution. I don't see any other issues pending for this scope.
One last check: does 'tests/test_helpers.py' need any cleanup regarding the old 'request.json' imports now that we have updated everything? I want to make sure no legacy tests are hanging around.
Run 'pytest tests/test_helpers.py' to be sure. If everything passes, you are good. Sometimes old test files have hidden imports that rely on deprecated behavior, so checking them is a smart move.
Running tests now. It looks like 'tests/test_helpers.py' was relying on 'request.json' in three separate test cases. I am refactoring those to use 'request.get_json()' instead.
Good catch. Refactoring the test suite to use the preferred 'get_json()' method validates that the internal API transition is smooth and doesn't break existing functional tests.
All tests passed locally. I am going to squash these commits into one clean PR and request the final review. This has been a long but very educational journey for my first Flask contribution.
Squashing is the right approach before the final merge. It keeps the history clean. You have handled this PR with the precision of a core maintainer.
The squash is done and the branch is updated. Everything is ready. I feel confident about the quality of these changes for the community.
Excellent work. You have helped move Flask toward a more modern and consistent API. Don't hesitate to tackle other open issues when you have time.
Thank you for all your help throughout this process! I'm going to mark this as ready for review. See you around the Flask project.
It was a pleasure collaborating with you. Good luck with the merge, and keep up the great work in the open-source community!

Wait, I just noticed a final CI failure in 'tests/test_basic.py' after pushing. It seems that 'flask.json_available' check is failing in the build environment. I thought I handled all those deprecated calls!

That is frustrating. Check the CI logs for 'tests/test_basic.py'. It is possible that a dynamic test setup in that file is still referencing 'request.json' conditionally based on the environment version.
You are right. 'tests/test_basic.py' has a helper method 'check_request_json' that uses an implicit getter. I missed that one because it was not explicitly in the main source path.
That makes sense. Rename that helper to 'check_request_get_json' and ensure it invokes 'request.get_json()' directly. This should align it with the rest of our refactor.
Updating the helper function now. I am also going to verify if 'flask/wrappers.py' has any remaining internal references to 'json' property that might be confusing the test runner.
That is a wise precaution. In 'flask/wrappers.py', ensure the 'Request' class properties are cleanly defined so that 'get_json' is the primary entry point for JSON payloads.
I found it! There was a property decorator in 'flask/wrappers.py' that was still wrapping 'request.json'. I have removed it and adjusted the tests to point to the new method.
Perfect. Deleting that redundant property decorator is the final step to ensuring 'request.json' is fully deprecated. Re-run your local tests to verify no regressions.
Running 'pytest tests/test_basic.py' now. Fingers crossed! The tests are executing much faster now without the legacy property lookup overhead.
The speedup is a nice bonus. By removing the wrapper, you have simplified the request object lifecycle, which is cleaner for everyone using Flask.
Everything passed! I am pushing the final changes to the branch now. Should I reach out to the core maintainers on the PR thread again?
Yes, tag the maintainers on the PR. Summarize that you resolved the edge case in 'tests/test_basic.py' to ensure full deprecation of the 'request.json' property.
Done. I sent a message noting the fix. It feels much more robust now that the internal helpers in 'flask/wrappers.py' are also updated.
You have definitely increased the robustness of the codebase. A smaller footprint is always better for maintainability in a framework like Flask.
I'm checking the CI build again. It is currently running the full suite. It looks like it passed all 450 tests this time!
That is the green light we were waiting for. You have managed to modernize a legacy feature without breaking the existing API contract for users.
I feel much more comfortable now. Thank you for catching that last 'tests/test_basic.py' issue before I submitted the final PR update.
No problem at all. It is common to miss these edge cases, especially when refactoring core components like 'wrappers.py'. You handled it gracefully.
I am officially closing the loop on this. The branch is updated, CI is green, and the maintainer just commented 'LGTM'. Thank you again!
That is fantastic news. Congratulations on your first successful, high-quality contribution to Flask! Enjoy the feeling of having your code merged.
It feels surreal seeing the 'Merged' badge on the PR. Since the deprecated 'request.json' is now handled, should I look into updating the 'flask/ctx.py' documentation to reflect this change properly?

Absolutely. Documentation parity is crucial. Take a look at the docstring for 'RequestContext' in 'flask/ctx.py'. You should explicitly note that 'request.json' is deprecated in favor of 'request.get_json()'.
I noticed 'flask/wrappers.py' still has the property descriptor. Should I mark it with '@deprecated' from the 'warnings' module, or just stick to the docs for now?
Adding an actual runtime warning using 'warnings.warn' in 'flask/wrappers.py' is the standard Flask approach. It ensures developers see the deprecation during development.
Good point. I'll add 'from warnings import warn' and update the getter in 'flask/wrappers.py'. Should I categorize this as a 'DeprecationWarning'?
Yes, use 'DeprecationWarning'. Also, make sure to set the 'stacklevel' to 2, so the warning points to the user's code, not 'wrappers.py' itself.
Implementing that now. I'll re-run 'tests/test_wrappers.py' to ensure that the warning is actually being triggered as expected.
Perfect strategy. Use 'pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning)' to verify the behavior. This keeps the test suite robust against silent deprecation failures.
The test failed as expected when I didn't include the warning, but passed once I added it to the property. This feels very clean.
Excellent. You are ensuring that every user who still relies on 'request.json' will get an actionable warning before the eventual removal.
Should I also update the documentation in 'docs/api.rst' to ensure the official Flask documentation matches this new behavior?
Yes, definitely. Keep the docs in sync with the codebase. Search for 'request.json' in 'docs/api.rst' and add the '.. deprecated:: 0.12' directive.
I found the section in 'docs/api.rst'. It seems straightforward to add the directive. I'll make sure to mention the alternative 'get_json()'.
That covers all the bases. You've handled the logic in 'flask/wrappers.py', the testing, and now the documentation. This is a complete contribution.
I feel like I've really grown in my understanding of the Flask internals through this process. Is there anything else I should check?
Review the 'examples/' directory. Sometimes developers copy patterns from there. If any example uses 'request.json', submit a follow-up PR to fix them.
Checking 'examples/tutorial/flaskr/db.py' and others now. It looks like most use 'get_json()', but one legacy script might need a tweak.
Spotting those legacy references is exactly what makes a contributor stand out. Update those files and submit a small follow-up patch.
Thanks for the guidance. I've updated the examples and sent the final patch. I'm really happy with how this whole issue turned out.
It was a pleasure guiding you through this. You've made Flask a better framework. Don't hesitate to reach out when you're ready for the next challenge!

Actually, I just noticed an unexpected import error in the integration tests within 'tests/test_appctx.py'. It seems my changes in 'flask/wrappers.py' caused a circular dependency during the 'app context' initialization. How should I approach debugging this?

Circular imports in 'flask/wrappers.py' are tricky. Check if your new 'request.json' deprecation warning relies on 'current_app' or other app-context-bound objects that haven't been fully initialized yet. Try moving the warning logic inside the property method itself rather than at the module level.
